Proteins

Proteins — sources, functions, essential amino acids, daily requirement and protein-energy malnutrition.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • List sources and functions of proteins
  • Describe essential amino acids
  • State the daily protein requirement

In simple words

Proteins are body-building nutrients. They are made of amino acids and are needed for growth, repair of tissues, enzymes, hormones, antibodies and fluid balance.

One gram of protein gives about 4 kcal. Proteins come from animal sources (complete) and plant sources (often incomplete).

Sources of protein

Type Examples Quality
Animal Milk, eggs, fish, meat, chicken Complete protein
Plant Dal, pulses, soya, nuts, groundnut Often incomplete; combine with cereals

Combining cereals (rice/wheat) with pulses (dal) improves protein quality — this is called supplementary protein action.

Functions

  • Growth and repair of body tissues.
  • Formation of enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
  • Maintenance of fluid balance (albumin).
  • Energy when carbohydrates and fats are insufficient.

Daily requirement

About 0.8–1 g per kg body weight per day for adults. More is needed in pregnancy, lactation, illness, injury and surgery.

🔴 Protein requirement

Adult protein need is about 0.8–1 g per kg body weight per day. Needs rise in pregnancy, illness, injury and surgery.

Where the nurse uses this

  • High-protein diet — encourage for wound healing, burns, surgery and infection, unless medically restricted.
  • Malnutrition — assess muscle wasting and oedema; refer to dietetics.
  • Kidney disease — protein may need to be restricted; follow the prescribed diet.
  • Patient teaching — explain protein-rich foods: milk, eggs, fish, meat, dal, pulses, soya.
  • Supplementary proteins — advise combining cereals with pulses for better quality protein.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Proteins are made of amino acids and are body-building nutrients.
  2. Animal proteins (milk, egg, fish, meat) are complete proteins.
  3. Plant proteins (dal, pulses) are often incomplete; combine with cereals.
  4. 1 g protein = about 4 kcal.
  5. Adult need: about 0.8–1 g per kg body weight per day.
  6. Proteins form enzymes, hormones, antibodies and albumin.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Supplementary protein action: cereals + pulses improve quality.
  2. Albumin maintains fluid balance; low albumin causes oedema.
  3. More protein is needed in pregnancy, lactation, illness and surgery.
  4. Soya is a good plant protein source.

📌 Memory trick

Complete proteins: “MEFM” — Milk, Egg, Fish, Meat (all animal, complete).

60-second revision

  • Proteins = body-building nutrients from amino acids.
  • Animal = complete; plant often incomplete.
  • Cereal + pulse = better quality protein.
  • 1 g = 4 kcal; need 0.8–1 g/kg/day.
  • Functions: growth, repair, enzymes, hormones, antibodies, fluid balance.

Test yourself

Which protein is complete?

Answer: C. Egg is an animal protein and is complete.

Supplementary protein action means:

Answer: B. Combining cereals (rice/wheat) with pulses (dal) improves plant protein quality.

Adult protein requirement is about:

Answer: B. Adults need about 0.8–1 g protein per kg body weight per day.

Albumin maintains:

Answer: B. Albumin maintains plasma oncotic pressure and fluid balance.

Which need more protein?

Answer: B. Protein needs rise in pregnancy, lactation, illness, injury and surgery.
